_hand_authored: Hand-mapped against public/hero/base-photo.png. UNLIKE hero-scene.json (generated by scripts/render-base-scene.mjs from a real camera) this plate is an AI-generated photograph with no camera to project from, so every number here was measured off the image with scripts/hero-grid.mjs and checked against a real composite via /hero-check + scripts/hero-shot.mjs. Edit it by hand, re-shoot, and look at the result — several of these corners were wrong by 2-4% on the first pass and only the composite showed it.
_geometry_note: Coordinates are PERCENTAGES of the plate (0-100), x rightward, y downward. lib/hero-regions.ts divides by 100 to reach the 0-1 fractions the compositor works in. Percentages because that is the unit the mapping grid prints, and hand-editing 41.4 is less error-prone than 0.414. Quads are topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft in TEXTURE order (corner i of the quad is corner i of the texture).

faces._plate2_perspective: THE SOLVE FOR THIS PLATE, in one place, because every wall number below is derived from it rather than eyeballed. Measured with a bilinear luminance probe, not read off a zoom. (1) BACK WALL CEILING LINE: strongest downward-brightening gradient in 13 columns from x=23.5 to 43, least squares y = 4.9885 + 0.11627x, max residual 0.12% — this plate's ceiling is genuinely straight, unlike the previous one's. (2) BACK WALL PAN LINE: darkest row per column, x=27..43.5, y = 89.0014 - 0.097911x, residuals under one pixel. (3) HORIZON is where those two meet: y = 50.60, vanishing point x = 392.2. The plate is 336px tall so its centre row is y=50.0 — the camera is level and its principal point is the frame centre, which is the assumption everything else leans on, and it falls out of the measurement rather than being imposed on it. (4) LEFT RETURN CEILING LINE: the diagonal running up and left out of the top of the frame, 10 columns x=19.4..22.1, slope 2.36552, max residual 0.18. It meets the horizon at x=40.39, so VP2 = (40.39, 50.60). (5) FOCAL LENGTH from those two vanishing points being perpendicular about the principal point: f^2 = (392.2-50)(50-40.39), so f = 56.7% of plate width, a horizontal field of 82.8deg. Wide, but that is what an interior plate looks like. (6) CAMERA HEIGHT above the pan, anchored on the back wall being 60in: project both of its pan corners onto the ground plane and set their separation to 60in, giving D = 42.15in. (7) VERTICAL MODEL, which is all the compositor actually needs: y = 50.60 + (y_pan - 50.60) * (1 - h/42.15) for a height h above the pan, on any plane, applied to that plane's own pan line. CONSISTENCY TEST: the ceiling solves to h/D = 2.18751 at the interior corner and 2.18753 at the right edge — two independently measured lines agreeing to five figures, which is not something that happens by accident. Ceiling height 92.2in above the pan.
faces._plate2_span_assignment: WHICH SPAN IS 60in AND WHICH IS 32in, settled by geometry rather than assumed. The alcove has three vertical boundaries: the room corner at x=15.05, the interior corner at x=22.2 and the right edge at x=44.49, so the candidates are 22.2->44.49 (22.29% of plate width) and 15.05->22.2 (7.15%). ASSIGNMENT A, back wall = the wide span: 0.371%/in against the return's 0.225%/in, the return foreshortened to 61%, an ordinary oblique view. ASSIGNMENT B, back wall = the narrow span: the return would be foreshortened to 17% of the back wall, a 10deg grazing angle, which contradicts its ceiling line falling at 2.37%y per %x — that is a steep recession, not a grazing one. B also fails outright on height: the back wall measures 79.2% of plate height pan-to-ceiling against 22.29% of plate width, a ratio of 1.53 once the 2.333 aspect is taken out, so a 32in-wide back wall would stand 48in tall. A gives 92in. A WINS. THE 32in IS THEN CONFIRMED THREE TIMES OVER, none of them the anchor: (i) the door's bottom rail at (38, 93.45) projects to 31.2in in front of the back wall; (ii) the pan's own front threshold projects to a depth of 31.4in; (iii) the pan is therefore 60 x 31.4in, which is a catalogue 60x32 base. The wall plane carries on PAST the enclosure to the room corner at 15.05, and that extra span is room, not shower — which is why showerWallLeft stops at the door post.
faces._alcove_corners: All four vertical boundaries found by sub-pixel darkest-column search, sampled at 13-17 heights each and reported with their spread, because a boundary that moves between samples is a shading contour and not a corner. INTERIOR CORNER: x=22.19 to 22.32 over y=4..62, a spread of 0.13%, so the whole line lives inside one pixel. Least squares gives 22.22 at the ceiling drifting to 22.34 at the pan — a lean of 0.12% over the wall's height, under a pixel, honoured only because it keeps the seam on the plate's own dark column at every height. Cross-check: the two ceiling lines intersect at x=22.09, 0.13% from the luminance corner. ALCOVE RIGHT EDGE: 44.486-44.500 at every height from y=26 to 82, dead vertical, no drift at all. (Rows y=58 and 62 read 44.27 and are excluded — that is the door handle, luminance 24 against the edge's 140.) ROOM CORNER, outside the enclosure: a thin dark line at 15.04-15.07 from y=2 to 62, also dead vertical. DOOR POST: left edge 15.82-15.94, right edge 16.44-16.46, core luminance 7-12. A vertical world line projects vertical only under a camera with no roll, and all four of these are vertical — the fourth independent confirmation of the solve above. WHAT THE PREVIOUS PASS GOT WRONG: it recorded the interior corner at x=31.2. There is a narrow dark line there, 1% wide with matched shoulders, constant at every height — but it is the sliding door's leading glass edge, not a corner. The real corner is 9% further left, and the broad luminance fall from x=18 to 22.5 that surrounds it (187 down to 91 at y=7) is the return raking away from the light, exactly the signature the previous plate had at its own corner.
faces._alcove_scale: Why these are separate planes rather than one warped sheet. Back wall 60in over 22.29% of plate width, left return 40in over 6.10%: 0.371%/in against 0.152%/in, so the return is foreshortened to 41% of the back wall's scale and one quad spanning both could not tile a 24in panel correctly on either. At 24in panels the back wall is 2.5 panels, giving joints at 24in and 48in from the corner; the return is 1-2/3 panels, giving one joint at 24in from the corner. The return's quad is ordered CORNER-FIRST — topLeft is the interior corner, not the outer edge — so tiling starts at the corner, a full panel terminates there, and the offcut falls at the outer end where the door post covers it. That is how the kit installs.
faces._panel_top_derivation: THE PANEL TOP FOLLOWS THE CEILING, at a fixed 0.30% clearance below the measured line, and that is a decision the numbers forced. 94.5in above the pan projects to y=5.61 at the interior corner and y=8.31 at the right edge; the ceiling there is 7.57 and 10.16. So a full-height panel overshoots this plate's alcove by 1.96% and 1.86% of plate height respectively — it would end ABOVE the ceiling. The alcove is 92.2in tall, so the honest install cuts 2.7in off a 94.5in panel, and the rendered field is 91.8in with the cut edge at the ceiling. This is the outcome the previous plate made impossible (there the panel fell short and stranded a band of bare wall), and it needs no departure from scale: heightIn is 91.8 on both planes and the vertical model reproduces it at the corner (91.87in), the right edge (91.83in) and the return's outer end (91.58in), all within a quarter inch. The 0.30% clearance is there so antialiasing on the top line cannot poke above the ceiling; at this plate's resolution it is one pixel. All plane tops meet at the shared corner vertex (22.20, 7.87) — one point, no step. RE-VERIFIED THIS PASS, on instruction to extend the panels to the ceiling, and the instruction turned out to be already satisfied. The ceiling line was re-measured independently — steepest luminance gradient in thirteen columns from x=24.5 to 44, giving y = 4.985 + 0.1221x against the banked 4.9885 + 0.11627x, which is 0.26% apart at the alcove's right edge and inside a plate pixel everywhere else. Against that line the back wall's panel top sits 0.17% below at the interior corner and 0.04% below at the right edge; measured on the RENDER rather than on the data, the wood begins at y=8.2 at x=23, 8.3 at 26, 8.7 at 30, 9.8 at 38 and 10.3 at 42-44, which is the authored line to within a third of a pixel at every column. The return is the same story: its panels run to y=0.2 at x=17.5 and 18.5, i.e. off the top of the frame, and pick up the corner line at 1.9 / 4.1 / 6.5 at x=19.5 / 20.5 / 21.5 against 1.5 / 3.9 / 6.2 authored. THERE IS NO BARE WALL BAND. What is above the panels is the CEILING PLANE — the camera sits about 50in below it and sees a great deal of it, which is why it occupies so much of the top of the frame and why it widens toward the alcove's right edge. It reads as a flat pale field because that is what a ceiling is; a wall-panel kit does not cover it, and painting panel material up there would put wall product on the ceiling. Worth recording that the plate gives no hard edge to argue with: a column profile across the ceiling line runs 102 at y=5 to 127 at y=12.7 with no step anywhere in it, so the line is a soft gradient and its position is only good to about a quarter of a percent either way. The panel top is as close to it as this plate can resolve.
faces._left_return_extent: showerWallLeft runs from the interior corner OUT TO THE DOOR POST at x=16.10, not to the room corner at 15.05. The post occupies 15.85-16.44, so terminating the plane at 16.10 puts the panel's outer edge underneath it: the post hides the termination and no sliver of bare plate can open beside it. Stopping at the honest 32in instead would land at x=17.42 and leave a full 1% of plate width of untinted wall standing between the panel and the post, which reads as a gap. So the plane spans 40in of this plate's 44in-deep wall — the same trade already made on panel height, for the same reason, and widthIn says 40 so the 24in joint still lands at true scale. ITS TOP RUNS OFF THE FRAME, and this time that is measured rather than worked around: the return's ceiling line has a real fitted slope of 2.366 and crosses y=0 at x=18.87. The previous plate used y=-17 because no ceiling could be found above the return at all; here the ceiling is found, fitted to 0.18% residuals, and simply leaves the top of a 2.33:1 crop. paintPanelTopEdge now clips the edge at the frame instead of dropping the whole segment, so the part still in shot is drawn as a product edge and the join at the corner reads.
faces._right_return_dropped: THERE IS NO THIRD WALL ON THIS PLATE, and the strip that looks like one is measured out rather than argued away. Profiles across x=43.8..47.0 at nine heights show the back wall's tone running flat to a shallow minimum at x=44.50, then a BRIGHT band rising to a peak of 180 at x=45.14 (against the back wall's 150 in the same row), then a hard dark line at x=45.92 that does not move by more than 0.02% between y=6 and y=84, then the vanity wall. That band is the brightest thing anywhere in the alcove, so it is lit from the vanity side, not from inside the shower. GEOMETRY AGREES: the partition's shower-facing plane sits at world X = -0.38 to -0.26 in camera-height units, entirely to the LEFT of the camera axis, while its outward normal points further left still — the camera is on its back side and that face cannot be visible at all. Whatever the band is (the partition's corner radius catching light, or the slider's right jamb), it is not shower interior, and multiplying a dark panel colour over 0.9% of the plate's brightest highlight would draw a black stripe down the edge of the shower. So wallColors[2] is a no-op on the photo plate: PHOTO_FACES still lists showerWallRight, this key is simply absent, the region resolves to zero faces and the compositor's own faces.length guard skips it. The Three.js plate is untouched and still paints all three.
faces._floor_perimeter: PAN OUTLINE, corrected in this pass. It is not the parallelogram the previous pass authored. The pan's back-left corner is the INTERIOR CORNER (22.34, 86.81), not x=17: left of the corner there is no back wall for the pan to meet, only the return, and the pan's left edge runs from that corner down and toward the camera along the return's own base line. FRONT THRESHOLD: measured at x=26 and x=30, the two columns the sliding door does not cover — the pan floor ends at y=94.75 and 94.45 respectively, and the line through them toward the back wall's vanishing point is y = 98.082 - 0.12106x. The previous quad ran (17,99.30)->(44.8,94.55), a slope of -0.171, which put the front edge 2.63% of plate height too low at x=30 and painted pan across the curb and onto the room floor. For x>32 the threshold is hidden under the door's bottom rail (a black bar falling from y=93.85 at x=34 to 92.65 at x=44), so it is projected rather than measured there, which is why the perspective solve had to come first. CORNERS: back-left (22.34, 86.81), back-right (44.49, 84.65), front-right (45.45, 92.58) where the front line meets the partition's base, front-left (17.80, 95.93) where it meets the return's base — behind the plant, so projected. The pan then measures 60 x 31.4in, i.e. a 60x32 base, and heightIn is corrected from 34 to 32.

showerFloor._note: THE CURB, added this pass, and it is the second face of the SAME region rather than a region of its own because it is the same moulded acrylic part in the same catalogue colour. The markup circled a white band across the bottom left of the frame: that band is the curb, and it was painted by nothing at all — the pan region stopped at the pan floor's front threshold and the room floor started well below it. TOP EDGE is the pan's own front line, shared corner for corner with the quad above so no seam can open between them. BOTTOM EDGE is the curb's base, measured in the warmth channel (R-B) rather than in luminance, because the acrylic and the plate's own flooring are within a few units of each other in brightness and 25 units apart in warmth: neutral 20-27 above the line, 39-50 below it. Eight columns from x=32 to 45 (left of 32 the base falls below the frame and right of 45 the partition takes over), then constrained to pass through the perspective solve's vanishing point at (392.3, 50.59) so it stays parallel to the pan's own front line: y = 103.64 - 0.13523x, reproducing the measured base at x=45 to within 0.06%. LEFT and RIGHT ends are the pan's own side edges extended down to that line, so the curb is exactly as wide as the pan. heightIn 5 is the curb's real rise; nothing reads it but the record, since the pan is a flat catalogue colour rather than a texture.

faces._floor_quad_note: RE-DERIVED FROM THE SOLVE, because the previous quad was four round numbers and it produced two of the three defects the markup circled on the floor. It ran (45,90.5)-(100,91.5)-(112,105)-(8,106), and (a) its LEFT EDGE, the line from (45,90.5) down to (8,106), cut a diagonal straight across the partition's base and across the shower's front — everything left of that diagonal was simply not painted, which is the bare wedge at the pan/partition/floor convergence, and everything above it on the partition's face WAS painted, which is the band of flooring running up a wall; and (b) its NEAR EDGE sat only 5% of plate height below the frame, so the last few inches of floor before the bottom of the picture were carrying almost none of the texture's rows and rendered as a smear. THE FLOOR PLANE, SOLVED. Floor lines parallel to the back wall all meet at the vanishing point the perspective solve already fixes: the pan's back edge (y = 89.0014 - 0.097911x) and its front threshold (y = 98.082 - 0.12106x) intersect at (392.3, 50.59), which is the horizon and the same point _plate2_perspective reports. Depth follows from the offset below that horizon being inversely proportional to distance: the two pan lines are 31.4in apart in the world and their offsets at x=50 are 33.52% and 41.44% of plate height, so the camera is 132.8in from the threshold and 164.2in from the back wall. CHECK, and it is the reason to trust the rest: a camera 42.15in above the pan with the solve's focal length (56.7% of plate width) predicts the back edge's offset at 33.96% against 33.52% measured — 1.3%, from two numbers that were derived independently. FAR EDGE is then the floor line through y=88 at x=50, which is a depth of 149.1in and sits above every point the clip allows. NEAR EDGE is the line through y=112 at x=50, a depth of 90.8in, which is 12% of plate height below the frame — that is what gives the front of the floor its texture rows back. Depth between them is 58.3in, hence heightIn 58. SIDE EDGES converge on the OTHER vanishing point, the one for lines running away from the camera, at x = 50 - f^2/(392.3-50) = 40.61 — and the left return's ceiling line, measured independently in Phase 1, gives 40.39. That 0.5% agreement is the check on the whole construction. widthIn is 255 because that is genuinely how wide the floor is where the far edge crosses it: an 82.8deg lens at 149in spans 255in, and the room's nominal 120in is the room, not the field of view. The tile count follows honestly — 36 planks of 7in across the far edge, 28 across the bottom of the frame.
faces._vanity_scale: VANITY-SIDE PIXELS PER INCH, derived on the vanity side and not borrowed from the shower solve, because this plate is generative and the two halves do not agree. COUNTER SPAN: the warm counter material starts at x=49.14 and ends at x=77.33, found in the R-B channel at plate-pixel resolution (wall 19-26, wood 55-80, the step landing inside one pixel at both ends and at every height of the band). That is 28.19% of plate width, 221.0px. ASSIGNED 61in — a 60in cabinet run, which is the largest size the vanity program sells (VANITY_SIZES tops out at 60) and the only one that fits a plate showing a door, three drawers and a second door, plus a 1/2in overhang at each end. So 3.62 px/in, i.e. 0.4622% of plate width per inch, and that is the number every countertop tile size is scaled against. CROSS-CHECK on the cabinet rather than the counter: the cabinet's own hard edges sit at x=49.63 and x=76.71, a 27.08% span, and 60in across that gives 3.54 px/in — 2.4% under the counter figure, which is the plate's own tolerance and not a decision to make. CROSS-CHECK vertically, and this is where the plate stops being consistent: the cabinet face stands 28.06% of plate height for a nominal 31in, i.e. 3.04 px/in, and the backsplash band stands 4.82% for a nominal 4in, i.e. 4.05 px/in. Three estimates spanning 14% either side of 3.62. THE HORIZONTAL ONE IS THE ONE TO USE, because the dimensions that drive tiling — the counter's 61in run and its 22in depth — are both horizontal, and because it is the only one measured against a span rather than against an assumed product height. For comparison the shower's back wall runs 0.3715% per inch, so the vanity draws an inch 24% larger; the counter being nearer the camera is most of that and the plate's inflation is the rest.

vanityFace._note: BOTH ENDS RE-MEASURED, and both moved. LEFT: the previous 49.6 stopped at the far side of the reveal between the partition and the cabinet — a genuine 0.5%-wide dark gap in the plate, 3.7px, running dead vertical from y=59 to y=90 (darkest column 49.265-49.270 at fourteen heights, spread 0.005%, which is a fifth of a pixel). Leaving that gap untinted was right while the cabinet was a mid tone and wrong once a dark colour was picked: the gap then renders LIGHTER than the cabinet beside it and the junction inverts, which is the 'reads open' in the markup. The face now starts at 49.14, the partition's own face, so the reveal takes the cabinet's colour and multiply keeps it proportionally dark; the vanityLeft seam redraws the crease on top. RIGHT: the cabinet ends at x=76.71, not 77.3 — a hard dark line, luminance 34-38 against 71-78 on the cabinet side, dead vertical from y=60 to 76 (below that the toilet crosses it). The old 77.3 is the COUNTER's right end, and running the cabinet out to it painted 0.59% of plate width of the shadow gap beyond the cabinet as though it were cabinet. TOP: the cabinet face begins under the counter's shadow band at y = 61.058 - 0.02917x, half a percent below the counter's own bottom edge. BOTTOM is the toe line, below.

THE TOE BOARD, added this pass as the cabinet's second face. It is the recessed board between the door fronts and the floor, it is the same cabinet in the same colour, and leaving it as bare plate is what made the cabinet float. The mechanism is worth stating because it is the same one that spoiled the left reveal: in the PHOTOGRAPH the recess is darker than everything around it — 95-143 against a cabinet face at 187-191 and a floor at 166-181 — so it reads as shadow. Tint the face dark and paint the floor dark and leave the recess alone, and the recess becomes the BRIGHTEST thing in the group; the ordering inverts and a shadow turns into a light stripe under the cabinet. Painted with the cabinet's colour it stays proportionally darker than both, which is the contact the markup was asking for, and it costs nothing to get right because multiply is doing the work. TOP EDGE is the toe step, shared with the face above. BOTTOM EDGE is the floor line the flooring's own clip now starts on, so the two meet without a gap: 1.9% of plate height at the left end and 1.8% at the right, which is the 3.5in recess at this end of the room.

faces._counter_bands: THE COUNTER IS FOUR BANDS, NOT TWO, and separating them is what this pass is mostly about. Every boundary below was found per column at plate-pixel resolution and fitted; the faucet's dark mass (x 58.4-64.2) and the basin (x 60-70) are excluded from every fit. B1, SPLASH TOP, in the warmth channel because the wall above is neutral and the wood is not: y = 51.8245 - 0.00093x, which is flat to within a third of a pixel over the whole run and is carried as flat rather than pretending to a slope this plate cannot resolve. B2, SPLASH BOTTOM = COUNTER SURFACE TOP, in luminance, where the shaded vertical splash gives way to the lit horizontal top: y = 57.5377 - 0.01904x, worst residual 0.137. B3, COUNTER SURFACE BOTTOM = FRONT EDGE TOP, the drop off the lit top onto the nosing: y = 58.4505 - 0.02018x, worst residual 0.062, the cleanest line anywhere on this plate. B4, WOOD BOTTOM, back in warmth as the nosing gives way to the shadow under the counter: y = 60.581 - 0.02995x, worst residual 0.226. WHAT THAT MAKES THE PLATE: a 4.82% splash, a 0.86% counter surface and a 1.65% front edge at the left end. THE FRONT EDGE IS A 1.25in SOLID SURFACE TOP: 1.65% of plate height against the splash's own 1.205% per inch is 1.37in, and against the counter-span scale 1.53in. Nothing needed tightening geometrically — the plate photographs a normal solid-surface nosing. What was wrong is that ONE quad covered both the surface and the nosing and mapped 22in of counter depth across the pair, so the nosing rendered about eleven inches of grain down a face that is an inch and a quarter tall. That is the butcher block. The two are separate faces now, each with its own real height. WHAT THE PREVIOUS PASS GOT WRONG, in numbers: the splash was authored 51.8-55.8 at the left and 52.6-55.4 at the right, against 51.78-56.60 and 51.75-56.07 measured, so its bottom floated 0.8% above the counter along the whole run (the gap the markup circled at the left end) and its top dropped 0.85% at the right end, opening a wedge of bare wall above it. The counter was 55.8-58.3, which starts inside the splash and stops 0.85% short of the nosing's bottom.

vanityBacksplash._top_is_computed: The top edge is NOT traced off the plate any more — see _splash_true_height. It is B2 lifted by a real 4in at the local scale, which is why the two ends differ: 4.51% of plate height at the left, 4.11% at the right, both exactly 4.00in.

faces._backsplash_ends: LEFT: the splash, the counter and the cabinet's reveal all start on the partition's face at x=49.14. There is no return at that end — the splash dies into the wall. RIGHT, and this is the miter the markup circled: the splash's front face ends at x=77.08 and a RETURN one to two plate pixels wide occupies 77.08 to 77.33, reading as a hard dark column (luminance 66-79 against 103-125 on the wood side and 124-141 on the wall side) with a rounded top at y=52.0 and running the full height of the splash and the counter. The previous side splash was authored 77.3 to 78.1, which is the whole 0.8% to the RIGHT of the return — it painted counter material onto bare wall beside the towel, which is why it read as floating. Both pieces now share the line x=77.08 exactly, so the miter has one edge and no overlap; the splashCorner seam draws the joint. The return is 0.25% of plate width for a 4in-deep piece, i.e. foreshortened to about 5% — the camera is very nearly in its plane, which is also why it is dark: no light reaches that face.
faces._counter_edge_note: THE NOSING, as its own face. 61in of counter by 1.25in of edge — the standard solid-surface build-up — so the material tiles 1.25in of sheet down it instead of the 11in the single-quad version was stretching there. It is the second face of the vanityTop REGION, not a region of its own: it is the same slab, the dealer picks it once, and lib/hero-regions joins both names under vanityTop so one selection paints both. Its top edge is shared corner for corner with the surface above and its bottom is the measured B4, so no plate can show between them.
faces._backsplash_note: THE PLATE HAS A SPLASH, and two passes were authored on the assumption that it does not. It is 4.82% of plate height of the same wood as the counter, standing on the counter's back edge from y=51.78 down to 56.60 at the left end, and it is separated from the counter's lit top surface by a luminance step of 30 to 40 units at every column. The reason it was missed is that the whole assembly reads as one warm band in luminance — splash 163-182, nosing 146-178 — and only splits cleanly in the warmth channel and on the step at B2. What the region draws is therefore the plate's own splash recoloured, not an invented one, which is why its bottom edge sitting 0.8% high was visible as a gap rather than as a slightly short splash. HEIGHT SCALING is unchanged in principle: the region is authored at 4in and the compositor scales it about its bottom edge, so a 6in selection stands half again as tall. Above the plate's own 4in the extra band lands on wall rather than on wood and reads a shade cooler; that is inherent in drawing a taller splash than the photograph has, and it is the same trade the 6in option has always made.
faces._vanity_top_gap_note: THE SHADOW BAND UNDER THE COUNTER used to be left as plate — the cabinet face began at y = 61.058 - 0.02917x, half a percent below the counter wood bottom at B4 = 60.581 - 0.02995x. A coverage sweep found it: rendering the plate under two configurations whose every selection differs and diffing them, the band x 49.5-76.0 y 58.3-59.5 came out identical in both, which means no material touched it. Left as plate it inverts the same way the toe recess and the left reveal did — in the PHOTOGRAPH it is the darkest thing between the counter and the cabinet, and once the cabinet is tinted dark it becomes the lightest. The face now starts on B4, so the shadow takes the cabinet colour and multiply keeps it proportionally dark.
faces._side_splash_dropped: THE SIDE SPLASH IS GONE, and what it was drawing is now drawn by the back splash plus multiply. The return is real — a hard dark column at x 77.20-77.34, luminance 66-79 against 103-125 on the wood side and 124-141 on the wall side — but it is TWO PLATE PIXELS wide, 0.25% of plate width for a 4in piece seen at about five degrees off its own plane. A face that narrow cannot carry a texture: the compositor built it a surface canvas clamped to the minimum, warped a 0.25%-wide sample of the counter scan onto it, and what came out was the sheet grain smeared vertically down a bright sliver standing proud of the splash beside it. That is the artifact in the markup. The back splash now runs the full 49.14 to 77.33 and the plate does the rest: its own dark return column survives multiply, so the return reads as a shaded return rather than a lit one, and the splashCorner seam at x=77.08 draws the joint. One region fewer, no sliver, and the read comes from a measurement instead of from a texture sample too small to mean anything.
faces._splash_true_height: THE SPLASH TOP IS COMPUTED FROM INCHES, NOT TRACED. Two passes traced the plate's own baked splash top (B1, flat at y=51.78) and called the result 4in. It is not 4in: B1 is FLAT while B2, the counter's back edge it stands on, falls 0.53% across the run, so the plate's splash is a wedge — 4.82% at the left end and 4.31% at the right, which at the vanity's own scale is 4.47in and 4.00in. A 6in selection multiplied that wedge by 1.5 and rendered 6.7in at the left. Worse than either number is the SHAPE: a flat top over a falling counter diverges from every other line in the assembly (B2 -0.019, B3 -0.020, B4 -0.030, the toe -0.108), and that divergence is what reads as 'too tall' long before the inch count does. _clip_note: Where a texture is ALLOWED to land, as against the quad which says how it warps. This plate has no rendered ID mask (the Three.js scene had one), so occlusion is hand-traced instead. First polygon of each list is the outer boundary; a polygon nested inside another punches a hole, via the even-odd fill rule. A HOLE MUST LIE ENTIRELY INSIDE ITS OUTER POLYGON — even-odd counts crossings, so any part of a hole that pokes out the other side flips back to filled and paints where nothing should. That is why the plant cut-out below stops just short of the wall's bottom edge instead of running past it. Traced deliberately tight: under-covering leaves a sliver of plate showing, which reads as shadow; over-covering smears material across a plant or a toilet, which reads as broken.
_plant_note: The plant cut-out in backWall is the one place a polygon is the wrong tool. A fern has no outline, so this is a compromise between two visible failures: too tight and wall material paints stripes across the leaves, too loose and a grey wedge of bare plate opens up beside them. It is tuned to hug the dense core and let the sparse outer fronds take a little bleed, because bleed on a few leaf tips reads as shadow while the grey wedge reads as a hole. A per-pixel mask keyed off the foliage's green would beat this outright and is the obvious next step if it ever needs to be better.

The plate already carries its own corner darkening and multiply passes it straight through, so these are deliberately WEAKER than what is measured. MEASURED ON THIS PLATE, at y=30: the interior corner reads 150.2 at its darkest column against a smooth interpolation of its immediate neighbours at ~154, so the LOCAL crease is only about 4 units, 3% — the big fall from 178 at x=20 is the return's own shading, which multiply already carries. The right edge reads 147 against shoulders of 150 and 154, also about 4 units but over 0.3% of width rather than 3%. Strengths below are set near those measurements rather than imported from the previous plate, whose corner was three times deeper. `from`/`to` are the corner's endpoints and `halfWidthPct` the fade distance either side, both in plate percent. WHICH ARE PAINTED: alcoveInterior and alcoveRight after the wall pass; curbFloor after the pan; vanityLeft, vanityRight and vanityToe after the cabinet AND the floor, because two of the three divide the cabinet from the floor and would be painted over otherwise; splashCorner after the splashes. The previous pass measured the vanity three and painted none of them — the compositor's only call was on a key named `partitionFloor` that does not exist here, so it was a no-op every frame. That is why the cabinet floated and why both of its junctions read open: the coordinates had been corrected and nothing was drawing on them. panWallLeft stays unpainted and stays as the record.

_fixture_note: Boxes around the plate's baked-in matte-black hardware, for recolouring it to the dealer's selected finish. A group is one finish CHOICE and carries a list of PARTS, because the sliding door's hardware is one choice spread over fourteen separate pieces of metal. Each part is a box in plate percentages [x, y, w, h] plus the two numbers that decide which of its pixels are metal. CUTOFF AND FEATHER ARE PER PART, and that is the correction this pass makes. They used to be two globals — 112 and 12 — and 112 was above the fixture/background valley for EVERY group on this plate, which is why bright finishes smeared: the boxes were tinting the surface the fixture sits on as well as the fixture. Measured by Otsu on each part's own luminance histogram, computed twice — on the box alone, which biases low where the part nearly fills its box, and on the box grown by 0.6%, which biases high where it does not — and averaged. The valleys land between 77 and 109 depending on what the part sits on: 87 for the faucet against a lit countertop, 104 for the track span that crosses the door's glass lap, 109 for the left hanger. FEATHER is 0.35 of the span from the cutoff down to the part's own 5th-percentile core, so the alpha ramp covers roughly the antialiased rim rather than a fixed twelve units. It is deliberately not wider: at half the span the fixture's own mid-tones go part-transparent and the wall shows through the metal, which is what a previous pass hit at 26 against the old cutoff. MATTE BLACK IS UNAFFECTED by any of this — it has no entry in FINISH_TINTS, so no patch is built at all and the plate shows through untouched.

So the escutcheon is a tall narrow oval and the lever is a short horizontal bar crossing its right-hand side, and the single 3.7 x 8.6 box that used to cover both was three-quarters empty. The empty part was harmless — those pixels sit above the cutoff and tint nothing — but it is not what the box was for, and a box that is mostly empty is a box nobody can check. HOW MUCH OF THE BLOB THIS FIXES: not much on its own, which the render confirms. The blob is a TONAL problem, not a footprint one — see the shade normalisation in the compositor. What the tight boxes buy is that the soft shading around the fixture, which runs 80 to 112 and is not metal, is now mostly outside the boxes rather than inside them being recoloured to nearly full strength.

_anchor_note: The anchors below are used ONLY by the Three.js fallback plate and are stale against this photo plate; the photo plate recolours the baked-in fixtures above instead of pinning product photographs. They are kept because that fallback still pins photos, and because the measurements are the record of where the plate's fixtures actually are. The plate has matte-black fixtures baked in. A product photo is pinned OVER each one and has to cover it outright, because multiply can darken the black blob but can never erase it. unitPerIn is therefore sized from the measured pixel footprint of the baked-in fixture, not from room geometry — this plate is generative and is not dimensionally consistent (solving its shower head and valve heights together puts the floor at 115% of frame).
_anchor_sizing: Solve unitPerIn = targetWidthFraction * plateAspect / (sizeIn * PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO * contentFraction), where plateAspect is 784/336 = 2.3333 and targetWidthFraction is the product's wanted width as a fraction of plate WIDTH. contentFraction is the share of the catalog frame the product actually fills, and it is the term that matters: scripts/measure-fixtures.mjs finds these three shots filling 94-100% of their frame, NOT the 1/1.5 that PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO assumes, so every overlay drew about 1.5x too large until this was measured rather than trusted. PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO is left at 1.5 because the Three.js plate's anchors were tuned around it and changing it would silently resize the fallback; it is divided back out here instead. Re-run measure-fixtures.mjs if the catalogue's crop ever changes. sizeIn is whatever the caller resolves from the component catalogue — 6in shower head, 6.5in trim, 8.9in faucet.

_door_glass_alpha_note: ALPHA 0.22, and ONE value serves a dark wall, a light one and a mid one, because screen is self-limiting: it adds in proportion to (255 - destination), so a near-white panel takes almost nothing while a dark one takes the whole reflection. Predicted lift, plate luminosity about 150 in the glazed field: on a dark slat wall (destination about 95) +19, a 20% lift; on a light Durasein sheet (destination about 205) +6.5, 3.2%. TUNED BY RENDER at 0.28 and 0.18. 0.28 flattened the dark slat panel — the wood lost its richness and the difference between the glazed field and the bare wall above the track read as a wash rather than as glazing. 0.18 held the wood but only just carried the leading edge. 0.22 sits between them. The light case never failed at any of the three, which is the self-limiting property doing its job, so no per-polygon alpha and no brightness weighting were needed.

It made things WORSE, and the reason is diagnostic — the tinted bar came out exactly as tall as the boxes, which means the boxes were nearly full, which means the box was never what was limiting the bar. It keyed the hardware at a cutoff of 112 copied from the compositor's old global and then feathered it with the same two box blurs the foliage gets. On a one-pixel rail that produces a band of high alpha four to five pixels wide running diagonally across the pan, and the mask restores the PLATE — so over a re-toned black base it painted the original WHITE pan back in a stripe, with the finish tint landing on top. The mask now reads its boxes and cutoffs from these parts instead of copying them, and feathers hardware in its own layer with one pass. RIGHT ANSWER B, the dashes: THE TONE STRETCH. The group stretch maps the group's 5th to 95th percentile across the shade range, which is what makes a shower head read as metal. Along this rail's centreline the plate's luminance swings 22 to 46 — compression noise on a one-pixel feature, not modelling — and the stretch turned that into a rendered swing of 80 to 150, i.e. the dashed line. The part now carries a fixed shade of 0.78 and opts out. WHAT IS LEFT is the plate's own rasterisation: a one-pixel line falling one pixel every twenty-one shows its staircase at 3x magnification whatever is done to it. At the hero's own size it reads as a rail.
_shower_base_note: HOW A CATALOGUE COLOUR IS PUT ONTO THE PLATE'S WHITE PAN, and why it is not a multiply any more. THE PROBLEM, measured: sampling the pan floor and curb inside their own polygons, the plate runs p25=143, p50=160, p95=184 — a 41-unit working range carrying the curb highlight, the fall across the pan floor and the drain. Rendered, the share of that range surviving the tint was 0.98 for white (a no-op), 0.89 for beige, 0.73 for grey and 0.29 FOR BLACK. Black lost seven tenths of the pan's modelling, which is the flat muddy hole the markup circled. THE OLD MECHANISM made that inevitable: multiply to a mid grey, then lay the target black over it at 62% opacity — and that second pass is an opaque fill, so it throws away 62% of whatever contrast the first pass preserved. WHAT THE MULTIPLY GETS WRONG PHYSICALLY: a pan's brightness is diffuse reflection plus specular gloss, and only the DIFFUSE part scales with the base colour. Acrylic is glossy whatever colour it is moulded in, so a black pan keeps its highlights nearly whole while its body goes dark. A plain multiply scales both, taking the highlights down with the body, and mud is the only place that can land. THE MODEL: out = factor * L + spec * max(0, L - knee), per channel. `factor` is the catalogue colour over the WHITE pan's own hex rather than over 255 — the plate photographs a white pan at a median of 160, so 160 is what white looks like under this light and every other colour is a ratio against it. `knee` is 169, the pan's own p75, where the diffuse field ends and the gloss begins. `spec` is how much of that gloss survives, and it rises as the colour darkens because that is where the highlight is doing all the work. Tuned by render at the values below. WHITE HAS NO ENTRY and is a no-op: the plate is already a white pan and painting it could only dull it. Applied as a 1:1 recolour of the plate's own pan pixels clipped to the pan polygons, not as a warped surface — there is no texture to map here, only the photograph to re-tone.

_layer_interaction_pass: PHASE 8, AND EVERY DEFECT IN IT WAS ONE LAYER REACHING INTO ANOTHER RATHER THAN A POLYGON IN THE WRONG PLACE. The single rule that came out of it: THREE PASSES PUT PLATE PIXELS BACK OVER PAINTED MATERIAL — the occlusion restore, the glass screen and the fixture tint — and all three are only meaningful where the plate still SHOWS through what was painted, i.e. under a multiply. The shower base is the one surface composited differently: buildBasePatch REPLACES the pan with the plate's own pan re-toned. Put raw plate back over that and you are not restoring anything, you are undoing the re-tone. Both halves of FIX 1 are that rule applied twice, and it is worth stating because the next dark-surface feature will hit it again.
_rail_band_diagnosis: THE MUDDY BAND ACROSS THE BLACK PAN — diagnosed by rendering the black-base config four ways at the rail crop and measuring the pan floor above the rail in each. ALL LAYERS ON 61.6. OCCLUSION OFF 61.6. RAIL TINT OFF 61.6. GLASS OFF 29.1. The tint model predicts 28.2 to 28.9 for those plate pixels, so the glass pass alone was more than doubling the pan and neither of the other two moved it by a single unit. CAUSE ONE, the glass. Its polygons' bottom edges run y 92.31 to 95.69, and the pan's front threshold is y = 98.082 - 0.12106x, so the sheets cover essentially the whole pan floor. Screening the raw plate there re-adds the white the re-tone removed. Fixed by punching the pan's own clip out of the glass layer before it composites — not by lowering the alpha, which would have dimmed the reflections on the walls too. CAUSE TWO, the occlusion restore, invisible until cause one was fixed. The mask keys the door hardware on luminosity, and the bottom rail is ONE plate pixel of metal keyed out of a white pan with a feather either side; over a black pan those feathered pixels restore a 160 onto a 29, which is the row of pale blocks along the rail. Same mechanism as Phase 6's gold streaks, resurfaced because the base re-tone landed after that fix. Fixed by skipping the restore inside (pan clip AND a doorHardware part box) — scoped to the hardware boxes rather than to the pan, because the right-hand planter's foot overlaps the curb and is a solid occluder that must still come back. Skipping rather than re-toning is the same result by a cheaper route: the destination inside the pan already IS the re-toned plate. RESULT, measured at the same crop: pan floor 61.6 -> 29.1, rail band peak 104 -> 63, and the band now reads identical to the occlusion-off reference. White is untouched to the byte (no re-tone, so no exclusion); beige 145.8 -> 133.2 and grey 126.4 -> 109.1 were being lifted by the glass too and are corrected with it.
